To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the MLE of the drift of Brownian motion following the symmetric SPRT is asymptotically efficient and has an explicitly calculable variance.
(1) the bias of the MLE is of order $n^{−1}$, and (2) the variance of the MLE, when the SPRT boundary is finite, is of order $1/n$.
the maximum likelihood estimate of the drift of Brownian motion following the symmetric sequential probability ratio is asymptotically efficient.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (a) What is the maximum likelihood estimate of the drift of the Brownian motion after the SPRT is stopped? (b) What is the bias of the MLE of the drift? (c) How does the MLE of drift compare with the MLE of a Brownian bridge?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
for a symmetric SPRT, the MLE of the drift is asymptotically unbiased, asymptotically efficient, and has a finite variance.
the MLE of the drift is asymptotically unbiased and efficient for all values of the drift, including the case of a negative drift, when the boundary tends to infinity.
the MLE of the drift is asymptotically unbiased and asymptotically efficient, and the variance of the estimate is asymptotically equal to the Cramer–Rao lower bound.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the SPRT with a finite boundary can be considered as a good approximation to the MLE for the drift of Brownian motion.
the asymptotic variance of the MLE of the drift of the Brownian motion is the same as that for the maximum likelihood estimator of the drift of Brownian motion with fixed sample size.
we provide a complete solution to the problem of estimating the drift parameter of Brownian motion when the boundary of an SPRT goes to infinity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the MLE is a good estimator when the drift of a stochastic process is unknown and the boundary of the test is sufficiently large.
the MLE is not asymptotically unbiased.
